utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Moore:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could we have your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Zvezdana Polovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to ask you some questions, but I want to deal with certain preliminaries at the start. I think it's right to say that you were born in the town of Vukovar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born in 1965?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You attended school there which you finished, I think, in 1984?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Secondary school, yes, 1984.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I think it's correct to say you went to the university at Osijek to study mathematics and physics but you left in 1989 but you did not graduate. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1990 is it right that you started a temporary job at Radio Vukovar where the editor, Mirko Stankovic, approached you to work there because he had heard your singing voice. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, I think your job was in broadcasting as opposed to singing?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't wish to touch on a sensitive subject. You met your husband there who had worked as a technician for some 20 years. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, prior to the war - if I may use that phrase - in 1991, is it right that you continued living in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we deal, then, please, with what I will call mid-1991. Are you aware of an incident that involved 12 policemen at Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the date of that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. The 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did matters change in the Vukovar area after that incident itself?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In very brief terms, can you tell the Court what way things changed.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: People no longer trusted each other. Here first and foremost I mean along the ethnic lines. They went back to their houses and tended not to leave their houses much. After the killing of those 12 Croatian police officers in Borovo Selo, nothing was ever the same again. For me the war began when the first victims fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I wish to deal with the radio station itself. Is it right that the station was situated I think in the centre of Vukovar in Marsal Tito Street?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following that incident would it be correct to say that in your view the HDZ took over control of the radio station?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it changed its name from Radio Vukovar to Croatian Radio Vukovar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you had been employed temporarily July 1990; I think it concluded in the end of the year 1990. Were you re-employed in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, sometime in June 1991. That was when I was re-employed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I deal with Mirko Stankovic, who had been the general editor. In June 1991 or, shall I say, the middle of 1991, that period, did he remain as the general editor?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was that? Were you able to -- did you know why he was replaced?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Mirko Stankovic was a pro-Serb editor or general editor. After the HDZ took over control of the radio station, there was no place there for Mirko Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, with who replaced him. Do you know who that was? Josip Esterajher was the one who followed Mirko Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a reporter called Vlasejvic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Glavasevic, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's my pronunciation. It's Glavasevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Sinisa Glavasevic, yes, indeed. He was also an editor and a journalist with Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you describe your relationship with that particular person?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: In addition to being my work-mate, he was also a very good friend and he was my best man, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his role within the radio station?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: He was a journalist and an editor of Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members of staff existed at the Croatian Radio Vukovar in June 1991, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: About 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the format for the material that was transmitted by Croatian Radio Vukovar at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We transmitted live. I'm not sure what you mean. Are you talking about the various media, CDs, tapes, that sort of thing? We transmitted live, and we played certain songs from the CDs that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe its political balance with regard to the transmissions?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Prior to the 2nd of May, we tried to allay tensions throughout the area. We tried to meet everyone's tastes, the tastes of all the different ethnic groups living in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Afterwards, when it all became clear, when the war intensified, we were in permanent contact with the defence staff and we went out to the field for as long as we felt that our lives were still not in danger. I'm talking about late August and early September, after which time you were no longer exactly able to go out to the field or go anywhere, indeed. At any rate, we gathered our information from the hospital, from the staff, and by talking to those people who were out in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to deal, if I may, please, with what I would describe as the shelling of Vukovar. Can you remember the first significant shelling of Vukovar? Or the Vukovar area, is perhaps a more precise question.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. The first significant shelling occurred on the 4th of July, 1991. Vukovar -- or rather, Borovo Naselje was targeted from the direction of Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know about the shelling of Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: My parents lived there at the time. I, too, hailed from that town. I got married to a man from Vukovar, but previously I had lived in Borovo Naselje. I talked to them on the phone that day, and they told me that they spent the best part of the day in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever in Borovo Naselje when an attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. On the 24th of August when a plane attacked Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to tell the Court what damage, if any, was done as a result of the plane attack?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Bombs were dropped on the elementary school. I'm not sure how many casualties there were, wounded and dead. I don't have the information. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally this in relation to this topic. Between the 4th of July and the 24th of August, are you able to assist the Court in telling them how often Borovo Naselje was struck with shells or bombs?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It's very difficult to remember specifically, but I was in touch with my parents daily and they were complaining all the time that there was shooting. I'm not really very good with weapons, but I know that rifles were being used as well as pistols in addition to powerful explosions and shelling. I'm not sure how frequently, but I know that between the 4th of July and the 24th of August they spent most of that time hidden in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, your parents, as you have told us, were at Borovo Naselje. Did they remain there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No. I proposed that they come to our home at Mitnica in Vukovar, thinking that that would be a safer place for them to be. By this time, Vukovar had not yet been subjected to any severe attacks. They eventually moved to Vukovar to our shelter. However, the very next day, the 25th of August, Vukovar was also subjected to a plane attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, can you very briefly tell us the nature of the damage or where the damage occurred as a result of that air attack?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact location in Vukovar where the bomb was dropped. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on then, please, to the radio station itself. Did the bombing on the 25th of August have an effect on the individuals who worked in the radio station?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. Our offices, the editorial office of Radio Vukovar was on the first floor at Marsal Tito Street, 16. After this heavy bombing we realised this was no longer a safe place to be. So we went down from the first floor to the ground floor. There was no proper shelter in that building, so we sat down on the steps and laid down our equipment there underneath the staircase. I believe this was sometime in early September when we moved down from the first floor to the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The broadcasting centre or the aerial, if I may call it that way, where was the main broadcasting mast or centre located?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: The aerial was about 10 kilometres outside town, along the Vukovar-Ilok road, and then just at the turn-off to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you always able to use that aerial for your broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No. At one point in time it was no longer used. However, we had a spare mobile transmitter that we had received from Zagreb that we later used, and we continued with our programme, despite the fact that our original transmitter had been destroyed or occupied. It only took us a very short time to resume our normal activities by using the other spare transmitter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that the original aerial was in the direction of Ovcara. Do you know when it was that that -- it ceased to operate?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It was in the first half of September. I can certainly say that much, but I can't be specific about the date. I think about the 5th of September. There was a vicious attack around that time, but I can't be certain about the date. That was when we had to move and vacate the first floor, and that was roughly the same time that the transmitter could no longer be used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why it wasn't able to be used?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It just didn't function anymore. It's that simple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only broadcasters at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: At that time -- or rather, several days after the fierce attacks and after we had moved to that small shelter -- you can't really call it a shelter. It was just a small space underneath the staircase. The part of town known as Sajmiste had been taken. At night it was often the case and Sajmiste lies on hilly terrain that flares were being fired. There were clusters of these flares - I'm not sure if that's what they're really called - being fired illuminating the best part of town. At the same time as the town was being lit up like that, they would play Serbian songs, probably in order to intimidate us. They illuminated the entire town, and the music boomed throughout the town because they were using very powerful speakers or Tannoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what sort of material was being broadcast on the loud-speakers?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: You mean which specific songs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you can tell us the general flavour of the songs. Did it have an ethnic emphasis?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what they're called exactly. But it says something like: "Silver lining Serb cloth. Who's out there telling lies saying Serbia is small?" That sort of thing. I can no longer remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the location of the radio station, was it hit at any time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The building was hit. The building in which we were was hit. The building was hit, but the new transmitter was operational, the building located in Marsal Tito, number 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you then move to?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We moved into another basement, which was closer to the Vukovar Hospital. It was a wine cellar belonging to the company called Vupik. And it was called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, unfortunately the interpreters didn't hear the name. Could you repeat it again, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: In Vukovar internally, or locally, it was known as Vucedolska Kapljica. That was the name that locals used for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I just want to deal with October, and I realise it's an artificial division, but just to give the Court an idea. What was the intensity of the attack at Vukovar at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: There were several thousand shells. Naturally we couldn't count them all, but I had a feeling that every second from early morning until late in the evening, various parts of the town were hit. Detonations produced various sounds. It was immense, thousands and thousands. And they came from various directions, were fired from various types of weapons, multiple rocket launchers, guns, air raids, planes dropping bombs, snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to deal, if I may, please, with the transmissions. Was there any time when you ceased transmitting prior to the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. Around the 15th of October, as we had come into new premises, we had to organise our work. And we had local broadcasts for local areas three times a day, at 8.00, 12.00 -- or rather, 2.00 and 8.00 p.m. And broadcasts intended for a wider audience, Zagreb and elsewhere, was transmitted several times a day. At one point in time we decided to discontinue broadcasts to Zagreb, meaning that we continued with local broadcasts but no longer transmitted to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you broadcast to Zagreb? Can you tell us very shortly why that was.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Because our reports underwent censorship in Zagreb; that happened on several occasions. And we thought that if we discontinued our broadcasts to Zagreb, then that would cause some anxiety there because they were no longer receiving any information from us. Up until that time we were the only ones sending reports, and we thought that if we discontinued our reports they would do something in order to transmit our reports in their original state, as we had sent them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on now to the period before the 18th of November, so a period that's shortly prior to. Is it right to say that there were, as far as you were aware, discussions about an evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that negotiations on evacuation were conducted. In our basement, in this wine cellar, young men from the post office came, as did Dr. Bosanac and Marin Vidic, Bili. The post office man managed to establish telephone contact with Zagreb, and some negotiations were conducted from our basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From memory 15 years on, can you remember how often Dr. Bosanac came to speak on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We didn't have a telephone line. On the 17th or on the 18th, I believe, we knew that the town would fall, any minute, any hour; and it was then that the men from the post office moved into our basement and established the phone contact. I saw Dr. Bosanac then. Only on that day, in that basement, did we have a telephone connection with Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Dr. Bosanac was talking about over the phone?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac spoke about evacuation of population with -- who remained in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whom she was talking to?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. She spoke with Raseta, who was a JNA representative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear what Raseta was saying?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I remember one sentence very well. He said there would be no problems. Just leave the town for us and everything would be fine. All of you would be able to leave town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was it you were able to hear a telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It was very quiet in the basement. I'm not sure how many people there were there, perhaps 20 or so of us. I'm not sure. It was very quiet. The lads from the post office, once they got the phone line up and running, they either had a loud-speaker or an amplifier, something of that nature, which enabled us to hear what Raseta said. Dr. Bosanac addressed him with "Mr. Raseta." And the voice on the other side seemed to belong to him because I had occasion to hear his voice previously while working on the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we deal just then with the 18th of November. Is it right that you then left your location and moved to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was it you went to the hospital on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: The town fell on the 18th. The command left the town and went in to break through, and we believed that we would be safer at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "we felt" that you would be safer, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Radio Vukovar team, workers of Radio Vukovar, Sinisa Glavasevic, my husband, Vesna Vukovic, and myself. Three of our colleagues went in to break through, Alenka Mirkovic, Zdravko Seremet and Josip Esterajher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the hospital itself, are you able to say if negotiations were still continuing for the evacuation or not?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I heard that they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you eventually evacuated yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the date when you were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. The 20th of November, 1991. It took me two days to reach Zagreb, meaning that I arrived in Zagreb on the 22nd of November, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go further on, I want to deal with the morning of the 20th of November. Can you remember, approximately, what time you awoke?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We woke up in the morning at around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we woke up," who was that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: In a room which was assigned to us in the hospital. There were several mattresses, and in addition to the four of us from the radio station there were three doctors there as well. So there were a total of seven of us there. I don't know who woke up when, but it was at around 7.00 in the morning when all of us realised we were awake and we started talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody leave your room that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. We talked for a while, and then at one point Sinisa Glavasevic said he would go out to see what was going on and when we would set out. That was the last time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen him since?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, never again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that was the last time that you saw him. Can you, in general terms, tell us the time that you left that room that morning, please?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It was around 8.00. Vesna, my husband, Branko, and I left the room. We passed through a corridor to reach the back entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you went out of the back entrance, did you see anyone who spoke to you about your evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. When we left the building, the hospital building, on the left side there was a man in a uniform standing there. He said, Men to the left. Women and children to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe to the Court, please, this man that you saw.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I can. He was tall, slim, on the slim side. He had moustache and dark, black hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What height was your husband at that -- that day?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: 1 metre 80, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the man that you saw was tall, slim, and with a moustache. Was he that tall than that or smaller?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: As compared to my husband, he was taller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his name at the time you went out and first saw him?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: At the time, when I saw him for the first time, I didn't know his name. In the next 15 minutes or so, while talking, whispering to the women standing around me, I learned that this was Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that Major Sljivancanin, as we know him, told the group that men were to the left, women and children should go to the right. Did any of the women approach him or speak to him?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. Several women talked to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they ask of him?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: They asked him why he had separated men from women, why he had put them aside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he give an answer?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the answer he gave, please?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: He said, Don't you worry. They are going for a brief questioning to the barracks and they, the men, will follow you soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, are you able to say if you saw other soldiers in the area?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. There were several soldiers there, too. I couldn't tell you how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to distinguish whether they were, what I will call, regular JNA soldiers as opposed to paramilitary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: They were members of the JNA regular forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself see any paramilitary or irregular soldiers at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, not at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to assess how many men were separated from the women in that group?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I think there were about 30 of them, at least as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to describe whether they were injured or not injured?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. There were wounded, some heavily wounded, completely bandaged up. Yes, there were wounded, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you recollect how long you remained there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I think for quite a long time, perhaps even two hours. We, women, stood on one side, the men on the other side. We watched each other but did not communicate. But we stood there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see the men then taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. At one point in time they turned behind the corner of the street and disappeared from our sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know, of course, that there were negotiations underway and monitors became involved. Prior to those men being taken away, did you see any monitors or peace organisations?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: While the men stood in front of the hospital, there were no observers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the men were taken away, did you see any?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: After they had been taken away, yes. On the other side of the hospital, people started coming in, the monitors of the European community, journalists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that you had had whispered conversations with some of the ladies that the gentleman with the moustache was Major Sljivancanin. Later on that day, did you have any other conversation about that man's identity?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I did. First of all we boarded the buses, and then we set out from the city, and during that day and on the following day before we reached Zagreb and many times after that time, I heard the name of Veselin Sljivancanin many times, and naturally, during that day while I was talking to the women on the bus, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I deal with time intervals, and I know it's extremely difficult. From the time that the men were taken away, are you able to estimate the time interval before the journalist and monitors arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It was before the noon. It was late morning. That's how I would put it. If we left the hospital at 8.00 and then spent some time just standing there watching the men and then they were taken away, I'm not sure precisely what time it was, perhaps it was around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want you to guess. I'm just asking about the time interval between the time the men were taken away --

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: All right. On the 20th of November in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I deal then, please, with one final matter. You were with your husband that morning. Was he taken away with the men?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I saw his remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everybody. Cross-examined by Mr. Vasic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Ms. Polovina, let me introduce myself. I'm a lawyer. My name is Vasic. I'm one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Mrksic. Since both of us speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to make a pause before answering my questions so that the interpreters can interpret, and we will do the same after you give me your answers. Thank you. First of all, I'd like to clarify a technical issue with you. You spoke to the investigators of the Tribunal and gave a statement to them on the 16th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't think it was on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I made a mistake. It was on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This statement was composed in English and was later read out to you in Croatian, and then you signed it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When giving statement, you were warned that you should give the answers to the best of your ability to any questions put to you and that you should clearly distinguish between what you heard from others and what you saw yourself.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you complied with this warning throughout that process?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were born in Vukovar, that you lived there, that you completed our schooling there. You must have been quite familiar with the situation in this town and with the relations in that mixed ethnic community. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. I knew my closest friends and family members. I was a student in Osijek, which means that I travelled daily to Osijek between 1984 and 1989. So I communicated with the people who were close to me, and I knew them very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people you were close with, you socialised with, were they of diverse ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that in 1990 you started working at the Radio Vukovar. It was a temporary job until the end of that year. Tell us, please, while you worked there at the radio, did you come across information arriving both from the Vukovar area, from Croatia in general, and even the entire SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I did come across such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point in time you said that your temporary contract expired, and I would like to ask you whether you continued coming to the premise of Radio Vukovar after that.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's how it was until you were re-employed there in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to clarify something else you said in your statement. You said that the radio station was located in Marsala Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: The office of the radio station was in Marsala Tito 16, whereas the studio from which we made our broadcasts was in another location. In the main office we had a very small studio where we recorded news programmes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now it's clear to me. Where is Marsala Tito Street in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: In the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about this other location, the workers' hall, where the main studio was located, where is that?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: The office of the radio is in Marsala Tito 16 across from Zladna Delina [phoen], whereas the studio from which at the time we broadcast our programme in June of 1991 is located in the workers' hall, which is 300 metres away from the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that Vukovar was a mixed community with several different ethnic groups. Were you familiar with the political situation back in 1990 during and after the first multi-party elections throughout the former SFRY, including the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I was superficially familiar with the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You must know then that the HDZ won the Croatian elections?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unlike the results at the republican level, do you know who won the elections in the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that it was the party of democratic change that carried the day in Vukovar led my Ivica Racin, would that ring a bell perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I know that we had the party in our town, but I'm not sure if they won or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Vukovar Serbs voted for this party for the simple reason that they had no national party of their own to back at those elections, such as the Croats had in the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who the president of the Municipal Assembly for Vukovar was following the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent certain. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were already with Radio Vukovar at this time. Do you remember about December 1990 and the amendments that were made to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. In your interview to the Slobodna Dalmacija magazine on the 10th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar, you said that the atmosphere in town had changed as early as the beginning of 1991. Would that be a fair assessment of what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically what I said, but I remember the interview, the 10th anniversary interview. I just can't remember exactly what I stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do accept that, but can you tell us if it is true that the atmosphere in town was unsettled as early as the beginning of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us how you saw the beginning of that year. You say the atmosphere was unsettled. How did that show?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: People started discussing politics much more. I can't give you a set date, a specific date, and say politics had never been discussed prior to that date. But it was sometime in late 1990, the period that you have referred to, and then certainly the beginning of 1991. One could feel a change, and politics became the most topical thing to discuss for everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that only in the Vukovar area or did that also apply to Croatia in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I have no idea what was happening elsewhere in Croatia because I lived in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember a time early in 1991 when the -- when barricades were being set up?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Serbs, too, setting up barricades in Serb-dominated villages as well as Croats, in their own villages where they were, the predominant ethnic group? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Villages in the surroundings of Vukovar, to my knowledge at least, were predominantly Serb. I remember specifically. I had a friend, a lady friend, who lived in Borovo Naselje. I know that I couldn't go and visit her because barricades had been erected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know if barricades were erected also near the Slon cafe and the Zurich cafe in Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I can't say because I travelled that area with no difficulty. A barricade for me means you can't get through, and I did travel that area freely at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In my understanding, a barricade is where there needs to be someone who will let you through, not a place where you can't get through. All I'm asking is whether you remember any barricades there at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What, in your view, was the reason that these barricades began to be erected? What was this about?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I spoke to that friend of mine who lived in Borovo Selo. She told me about the fear that people felt there, that there were all sorts of rumours in circulation. Some people were even saying that they had moved their families, their women and children, by boat across the river into Backa. There was fear in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the propaganda in that village to the effect that the Ustashas would come to the village and kill all the children, slit their throats?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that was indeed what she told me, that propaganda was rife and that everybody was afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When someone drops the term "Ustasha," that probably reminds people of World War II and the horrible crimes committed by the Ustashas in Croatia. I suppose that's what the propaganda was about; it was a reference to that period in history.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I'm saying I don't know because I was only born in 1965. I don't know about the Ustashas. I've never seen one myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is precisely the reason why I'm saying that this reference to the Ustashas was a historical reference, a reference to a different time long ago. I agree with you in as far as I'm not aware of any units, military units, at the time that described themselves as Ustasha units. You mentioned this fear or apprehension that took hold of the Serbs of Borovo Naselje after all this propaganda work. They got so scared, in fact, that some of them moved their children and women and wives to a safe place across the river to Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I friend told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your opinion the war started on the 2nd of May, 1991, after the incident in Borovo Selo. You said this when prompted by my learned friend. You said that for you the clashes began the day the first victims fell?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall go back to the inter-ethnic atmosphere and the situation in Vukovar and the Borovo Selo incident as well as its significance. But what about the 1st of May, 1991, in Brsadin near Vukovar, what happened there? Stevan Inic was killed by Djura Gelencir, an HDZ member. Do you know anything about this incident?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I've never even heard those names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to Borovo Selo, the 2nd of May. Did you know that on that day more than 50 members of MUP's special forces, Croatian MUP special forces, entered Borovo Selo on that day and most of them were ethnic Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't have information that's nearly as specific. I know they were Croatian police officers, and I know that 12 of them were killed. When I say "killed," I mean dead. But there were some who were wounded as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were more than 12, because I think the answer you gave to my friend --

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. The way I remember it 12 were killed and a number of them were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the MUP forces entered Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May after the municipal authorities of Vukovar, led by the then-president, Stanko Dokmanovic, had reached an agreement with the locals to remove the barricades in Borovo Selo. It was once the barricades had been removed that the MUP forces entered Borovo Selo. Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you perhaps hear that the JNA put an end to these clashes by positioning themselves between the clashing parties?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know how the clashes happened exactly. I only know about the number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I had to wait up for the interpretation. You said in your statement that after these events in Borovo Selo, Vukovar and its surroundings were gripped by fear. People stopped going on trips, traditional trips, that were a daily reality and a very popular pastime in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by daily reality and popular. On the 1st of May, people went to Adica and Dzergaj, two popular destinations. On the 2nd of May, the killing in Borovo Selo occurred. And then you say after the 2nd of May people stopped going to these popular holiday destinations. Well, yes, we can put it that way, but I don't remember that particular 1st of May being a very merry occasion either. People didn't go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question had to do with the fact that under normal circumstances, people from Vukovar would often go to these destinations to be out of doors and to pursue some physical activities. My question is: Did they still make these trips to the surroundings after the 2nd of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know. I myself didn't go. I can't tell you about anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About after these events on the 2nd of May in Borovo Selo? Is it not true that barricades were removed in most localities throughout the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I know that this was the case with some localities. I couldn't say that it was most localities, and I don't think I would be able to enumerate for you all the Serb towns and villages in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Borovo Selo were there rumours again that a new group of MUP forces would be arriving? Did that -- did this cause additional panic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I have no idea what else people were saying in Borovo Selo. My only friend there was the one that I spoke to on the 2nd of May. After that I don't remember speaking to her again in 1991. We did hear from each other again several years ago, but not in 1991. That was the last time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an uncle and an aunt in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No. I suppose this is something you got from my statement. It's not aunt and uncle. I believe this is a matter of translation. It's my father's family. They had a cottage at Savulje. Savulje was a holiday resort near Borovo Selo. Yes, they were there; that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if after the 2nd of May, 1991, all traffic connections between Vukovar and the surrounding villages were cut?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I know that I was in Borovo Naselje at the time and that I wasn't able to go to Vukovar for a period of maybe three or four days. It was impossible to go. I couldn't drive -- I couldn't take a bus there; that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about after the 2nd of May, did people from Borovo Selo still go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, those whom you knew?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I only had one friend there, and she didn't go. I never saw her there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this a convenient time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can make it one, Mr. Vasic. We will adjourn now for the first break and resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break we spoke about the Borovo Selo events. Do you know whether after these events there were any attempts on the part of the president of the Vukovar Municipal Assembly and then also on the part of the prime minister of SFRY, Ante Markovic, and Admiral Brovet to reduce tensions in the area and to try to smooth the situation?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not sure you enumerated the exact posts held by these persons. I think that Ante Markovic was the president of the federal executive council, but you put it in different terms. I know that after the 2nd of May, several days later, he came to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the interview that I've mentioned -- or rather, in the statement, did you say that despite these attempts to reduce tension and to find a solution, a compromise, these stories started circulating around Vukovar and spreading panic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please clarify for us what kinds of stories these were and what reaction did they cause among population?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Everybody was afraid. I heard these stories from people in my circle, neighbours, friends. Senior citizens, some of whom had war experience, used to say there would be war. At any rate, everybody felt fear. People of my age did not have -- did not feel fear to such an extent. I personally couldn't fathom that something terrible, as terrible as what unfolded later, would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to Radio Vukovar where you worked. You have already told us that in May 1991 it was renamed into Croatian Radio Vukovar, that editor-in-chief Mirko Stankovic was removed due to his pro-Serbian orientation. Would you please tell us whether the director of Radio Vukovar, who was a Croat, was also replaced?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. After these events he didn't work on the radio any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was he replaced; do you know? Was he replaced due to his pro-Yugoslav orientation?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he was replaced or left of his own. I don't know whether he received any official document terminating his employment. Somehow I think that he left on his own. I think that he couldn't put up with the newly created situation and he simply left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number of employees and their composition, did it also change in relation to what it was before the -- May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that previously there used to be 15 employees and after May there were nine?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether these figures are correct, 15 and nine. I would have to go back and check it against the names that I remember, but roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a number of Serb employees of Radio Vukovar who left their work?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You received some reinforcements. From where did these people arrive?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: In June, once I was re-employed, an audition was organised. There was several young people who were hired at that time, perhaps five or six of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to five or six of you young journalists, was -- did Croatian Radio Vukovar also receive reinforcement in the form of two experienced journalists?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. If you were to give me their names, then I would be able to tell you whether they were experienced journalists or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Margareta Tot-Arvaj and Marija Sesler.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: These two ladies were hired at the same time after that audition. They had no experience whatsoever, and they were young girls of some 20 or so years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us something about how the work changed after it became Croatian Radio Vukovar. Can you tell us something about the programming. Was the content of the programming also changed?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. Before the 2nd of May, the programme was aired from 13 or 1400 hours until 1800 hours. After the 2nd of May, it was expanded, the air time was, and I don't know whether it was broadcast from morning until evening or perhaps throughout the entire 24-hour period. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this new policy -- programming policy that was introduced, did you become a reporter as well as a broadcaster?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: After this audition I was re-hired as a broadcaster, announcer, which is the same position I held in 1990. So I was an announcer in that local small radio station, and that entailed also selection of music to be played. As the war escalated, older employees were leaving the radio station and younger people remained; and thus, I also became a radio journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since becoming a journalist, did you have to meet certain requirements of the editorial policy in your work?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the OTP investigators, you said that in June of 1991, once you were re-hired as an announcer and a reporter, you had to do everything that was required of the employees. Could you now clarify to us exactly what was required of the employees.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I could give you some examples. I don't have a specific recollection, but the requirements were typical of those that the journalists had to meet. Why was the water supply cut off? When would it be reinstated, and so on. So there were a lot of such anomalies, if I can call it that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any requirements that the HDZ set in relation to political programming on your radio station?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, there were no particular requirements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the OTP, you said that the HDZ believed that a programme could be organised where various participants could exchange their views live, thus enabling the population of Vukovar to hear live the views of their political leaders?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Political leaders of the town would occasionally come to the radio station. Sometimes independently, sometimes several of them would come simultaneously. And then they would be given opportunity to state their views.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there came a time when before sensitive topics were discussed on the air, you had to seek approval of the defence committee?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time when you heard of the Vukovar defence committee?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I think that this was improperly translated. I don't think that we used this term "defence committee." It was a Territorial Defence staff or something to that effect. At any rate, those who organised the defence and were headed by their commander. This is what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it called the main defence staff of the city?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We could call it that, yes. We could say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was on the staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: At the time in June and July, it was Tomislav Mercep. I'm not sure about the dates when he was a member, but it was at around that time, June, July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was the commander. And do you know who else was a member of the Main Staff or did you perhaps have contacts only with him?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I can't remember the names of other people. I know who came after he was no longer commander. I know who his successors were, but who was a member of the staff along with Tomislav Mercep, I cannot remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us now that we have touched upon this subject, who was a member of this staff, the Crisis Staff, after Tomislav Mercep left and until the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: After Tomislav Mercep left it was Mile Dedakovic, Jastreb. And after his departure, the command was taken over by Branko Borkovic. Mladi Jastreb was the nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of cooperation did you have with this defence committee while it was headed by Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: As this was the very beginning of the war, all of us had to get accustomed to the situation, both us at the radio station and they, the defenders, so that initially we had some problems, but later on it became more coordinated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now turn to what you said to my learned friend, namely that for a while your parents stayed in Borovo Naselje and that you went to visit them there. Do you know that after these events in May of 1991 in Borovo Selo, in June and July, members of Croatian community organised themselves for defence against the local Serbs. And do you know whether this was organised on a street-by-street basis in areas where Croats constituted majority?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No. If you're referring to Borovo Naselje, I have no idea where Serbs constituted a majority. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in July in Borovo Naselje, pursuant to the instructions of Tomislav Mercep, a campaign was instituted to get rid of Serb residents?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that from the 2nd of May until the 4th of July when Borovo Naselje was shelled from Borovo Selo, in the Vukovar area there were no armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to agree with you on that. There was occasional exchange of fire. There was no intense shelling, but yes, there was firing. One could hear shots fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that precisely during this period of time, late June, early July, certain facilities, houses, and commercial premises owned by Serbs were blown up as well as newsstands of the Borba publishing agency from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I know that certain premises were blown up, but I do not know that they were owned by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about the Borba newsstand?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that certain residents of Vukovar went missing during that period of time? Was this discussed in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Nobody disappeared in my vicinity. Some members of my family fled, but as for people disappearing, no, I don't know about that. Nobody reported it to me that any of their dear persons went missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us go back briefly to the 4th of July, 1991. In the interview that you gave to Slobodna Dalmacija newspaper, did you state that only upon reaching Zagreb did you learn that this attack on Borovo Naselje had been provoked by a previous shelling of Borovo Selo from Osijek?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember. Are you sure that this pertains to the 4th of July and not to the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's your recollection in relation to this? Because my information seems to suggest we're talking about the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know. When I reached Zagreb, all the Croatian papers were writing about the 2nd of May. There was one or several articles suggesting that there had been active provocation from Osijek. I can't remember the specific newspaper that I read this in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to the 24th of August, 1991, which is another date that you mentioned. You said there was a plane attack against Borovo Naselje and that the elementary school building was hit. Did this elementary school building actually house the defence staff of Borovo Naselje at the time, its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: That was what I heard, but I wasn't there myself. I know that the local commune premises were inside the school building and so was probably the defence headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you perhaps hear that a JNA air force plane flown by Sasa Acimovic, a native of Borovo Naselje, was shot down over Borovo Naselje on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I know that Sasa Acimovic came from Borovo Naselje. He went to the same primary school that was hit as did I. His house is across the way from the school; the distance is perhaps about 100 metres. I'm not sure if the plane is shot down or not, though. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about any JNA planes being shot down on that day over Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I know that several planes were shot down. I'm not sure if on this day, and I'm not sure if Sasa Acimovic was in one of those. This is what I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, the pilot's name is Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, have you ever heard the story saying that the 25th of August attack on Vukovar had been preceded by a JNA plane being shot down? Have you ever heard the suggestion that this was what triggered the attack?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a journalist, were you aware of the fact that in May four brigades of the National Guards Corps were set up?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. I know that defence was being organised. I'm not sure what these units were called, if they were brigades; and if so, how many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that pursuant to President Tudjman's decision, siege was laid to all the barracks throughout Croatia, including the Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I could agree with what you're saying to some extent. So my answer is partially yes. I'm just not sure about all the barracks throughout Croatia, including the one in Vukovar. I'm not sure about the bit where you're suggesting that all were under siege.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you worked with Radio Vukovar, did you ever hear that there was an order from the commissioner for the town of Vukovar to cut the Vukovar barracks' electricity and water supplies and to cut their phone lines?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I heard nothing about that. In our section of town and among the people that we were in touch with at the time, it was a well-known fact that there was no water and no electricity. I'm suppose the same would have applied to the barracks. I must say I even find your question a bit strange. Because on the 20th of November, on my way out of town, along the stretch between Sajmiste and Negoslavci, that's where we were, and I was quite astonished to hear people suggest that, yes, they did have electricity because I thought there had been a general power cut or absence of electricity throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about Negoslavci, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that after the 25th of August you remained with your husband on the premise of Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout your time in Radio Vukovar you transmitted for Vukovar and for the whole of Croatia. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, our signal was only powerful enough, our transmitter was only powerful enough to cover Vukovar municipality, and a phone line was being used to forward reports to Zagreb. The signal was not strong enough to cover the entire territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you broadcast reports in addition to the facts you published, you said you also had to appeal to the public's emotions as well as keep in mind the reactions of the political leaders. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this period, you were receiving visits from foreign journalists and media, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Some were coming --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean September and October.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: September, yes. October, no. But in September, yes, we did receive a number of visits. But Vukovar was besieged and cut off by early October. I'm not sure if anyone arrived from Bogdanovci or Osijek. I can't remember specifically. In September, yes, there was a presence of foreign journalists in Vukovar. But October, I'm much less sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the journalist from the Corriere Della Sera? Do you remember when he came? When was that?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We were still at Marsal Tito Street. We remained there until the 15th of October, so that journalist must have visited sometime before the 15th of October, but I can't be specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the after the 15th of October when you moved and went to the Vupik cellar, as you said? Was there a rather considerable number of people from Sajmiste who arrived in that same location?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, but they didn't arrive the same time as we did. On the 15th of October we left our old offices. We were driving through town. I remember the workers' hall. But the first place we went to was the municipality building. They said it was okay for us to go to Vucedolska Kapljica, the shelter that was there. It took us several days to get organised, by which time those people arrived who had been Sajmiste up until that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is, roughly speaking, the time when Sajmiste fell?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. Based on my information, that would seem to be true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if certain soldiers, members of the ZNG and MUP, came to your studio to inform themselves about the situation that prevailed along certain sections of the front where they were not physically present?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Sometimes some people would come, but they were more helpful to us then we were to them because they provided information that we wanted and they told us a lot about stuff that we wanted to know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any members of the H-O-S, HOS, there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I never saw them myself, but I heard that a group of HOS members had visited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about these HOS members? Were they not the ones who held the most crucial portions of the Vukovar front line, as your colleague, Alenka Mirkovic, seems to be suggesting?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I really don't know about the deployment of Vukovar's defenders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told my learned friend that once you were -- once you had moved to the Vupik cellar, you started broadcasting news three times a day. There's something else I want to know about this. When was the first time you called upon the political leaders and the government to take responsibility for Vukovar's situation?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I think the first time I called them to account or we called them to account was in early November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that when your reports first began to be censored, following orders from the leaders in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: That may be the point in time. I can't be very specific, but I think, roughly speaking, the time-line would seem to make sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you could practically watch your own reports on TV, realising at the same time that they in no way resembled the original ones that you had dispatched, which only confirmed your point, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We did not have a TV set, and we were thus unable to watch our own coverage, our own reports. There was a TV set, the only one, at the headquarters. We would sometimes go there if one of our reports was being aired, and then we would have a look. We realised that our reports were being cut and curtailed severely by listening to the Croatian radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is very elucidating. Being critical, as you were, about the work of the government and the top leadership, you enjoyed the backing of the town's commissioners of the defenders and of the whole town?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: You mean we as a radio station enjoyed the backing of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of the reports that you were sending and what you were saying in those reports.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We enjoyed the backing of all these people and institutions that you have mentioned, and it was by joint decision that we decided to proceed as we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was raised at the time, was it not, that Vukovar may have been sacrificed for a higher goal, which begs the question if it still made any sense to transmit your radio programme.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not sure this was the point in time when the question was first raised, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the issue raised?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It was still -- we were still in Vukovar under siege when the issue was raised. That much is certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This issue was a logical result of the way the Croatian government treated Vukovar, a needy place facing a serious situation?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time - and I'm talking about November 1991 - did you enter into any polemic about the political objective that might have been reached by allowing Vukovar to fall?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the conclusion not just impose itself as part of this discussion that the fall of Vukovar or, rather, allowing Vukovar to fall and leaving Vukovar to its own devices, as it were, was the price for the recognition of Croatia, the price to pay for the recognition of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: You couldn't exactly call it a conclusion. We debated the matter; that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that President Tudjman had told Mr. Mercep that for Croatia it would be far graver if 200 people from Zagreb got killed as opposed to 2.000 people from Vukovar, who would have constituted less of a casualty?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I never heard of anything like that being said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that at some point in 1991 about 100 Serbs went missing in the Gospic area in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I was not aware of that at the time. I was in Vukovar myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear at some point later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, what relevance is that to the issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you suggest any, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honours. We talked about Vukovar's sacrifice, a price to pay for Croatia's recognition. This is the issue that I'm discussing right now. And my line of questioning ends with the following submission. My next two questions, the events around Gospic, and the fall of Vukovar, having to do with this epilogue, as it were, that I mentioned a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't immediately see any connection. Quite content that it's part of your case that Vukovar may have been sacrificed, but to bring in Gospic seems to be going too far. You could leave that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following your return to Zagreb, did you at any time learn that in late 1991 the European community complained to Croatia and raised objections about some things that happened in Croatian territory, saying that this might prove an obstacle on the path to Croatia's political recognition?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember that specifically. I arrived in Zagreb on the 22nd of November. All I did was search for my husband, who at the time was still listed as a missing person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's come back to Vukovar again. Can you please tell me whether you were subjected to censorship of information by the Main Staff of the Vukovar defence?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think so. Everything that we reported was, in a way, in agreement with them. We knew what we could report on and what we could not report on. We cooperated well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point during that cooperation, did you receive an order or a recommendation from Mr. Borkovic - I don't know what to call it - to stop broadcasting so that the problems of Vukovar could be taken seriously in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: The programme was broadcast continually for the local area, three hours a day from 8, 14, and 2000 hours, and some reports were sent out in agreement with Mr. Borkovic. And for a period, we did not send reports to Zagreb in agreement with Mr. Borkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So based on what you talked about with Mr. Dedakovic and based on the feedback you got from Zagreb, you understood that there will be no help for Vukovar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We hoped until the last day that help would, nevertheless, come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive information from Mr. Dedakovic that there would be no technical support or no other type of assistance had set off from Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I didn't receive any information from Mr. Dedakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you learned that the command of the Vukovar defence would leave Vukovar and that you thought about leaving with them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
