utterances.text: Are you thinking about these last days?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: The 17th and onwards, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you used the term "breakthrough" for this departure. Was that armed breakthrough or just leaving via the roads that could be used to get out of Vukovar, which were perhaps not just the ordinary, regular, routes?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It was not an armed breakthrough of any kind. All the roads, actually, were regular, normal roads, except for the fact that they were occupied. The term "breakthrough" was used in the sense that it was not possible to pass through. So that is why the term "breakthrough" was used. It would be an attempt to break through. Some managed to do that and some were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the events in Vukovar that we are talking about, the population was multi-ethnic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please help me with the time frame of this conversation and the departure of the Vukovar defence command. In your statement, did you tell the Prosecutor that on the 17th of November you heard that the command had decided to leave Vukovar and that Mr. Glavasevic on the 18th of November, at around 1400 hours, went to the command to agree the -- on the details with them, but he didn't find anyone there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: All of that was happening on the 17th and the 18th. We , and when I say "we," I mean the people -- us who were working on the radio. So on the night of the 17th and the 18th, we were talking about whether we would also attempt this breakthrough with the command or whether we would stay where we are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Glavasevic go on the 18th of November at around 1400 hours to the command to see?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about this 1400 hours. It's actually 2.00 in the morning, it's 2.00 a.m. and not 2.00 p.m. I know that it was night when we were discussing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to check my copy of your statement. It's possible that you said that it was 2.00 a.m. but it states in the statement 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Well, in any case it was night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say in the same statement that on that day, the 18th, your colleagues Alenka Mirkovic, Josip Esterajher, and Zdravko Seremet left?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, they did leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that night you stayed in the basement where you were joined by people from the post office, from the PTT?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these people Mr. Bozidar Zugec and Emil Aleksander; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't Emil Aleksander definitely because I think he was killed by a heavy shell. The other person was in a cellar or basement next to ours. The basement where we were was actually an extension of another basement. You couldn't go from one basement to the other, but we knew that a group of people was there and hey also knew that we were in our part of the basement. I don't remember when, but it wasn't on the 17th of November, definitely, it was much earlier. When I say "much earlier," I still mean November but it was probably early November when Emil Aleksander was killed. I think that it was a cannon -- artillery shell that fell. It was a heavy one. It killed his wife, small baby, his parents. I think that this one shell actually killed some ten people. So Emil Aleksander was not there on the 17th of November. Zugec, perhaps he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us that you heard a conversation or conversations and negotiations relating to evacuation. Did you tell the investigators of The Hague Tribunal that the negotiations lasted from the 18th until the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, if there's going to be questions - and I don't criticise the question in any way at all - but if there's going to be questions about what was said to the investigator, might I respectfully submit it's only fair that the witness have a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Polovina, if you would like to look at the statement to refresh your recollection for any of these questions, please indicate that and you can look at the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, if you need to see it, I have a statement or perhaps you do recall it.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I think I know what you're talking about. I think in one sentence it does say that the negotiations lasted from the 18th until the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when they began, but those last three days when we were in the hospital, the 18th, the 19th, and then the 20th, early in the morning, I heard that negotiations were being conducted. Before that, before we went to the hospital while we were still in the basement, there was also that part of the negotiations that I personally heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. I'm interested in that part when you came to the hospital. You said that you were in the basement and that at one point on the 19th of November, if I concluded correctly, you saw a person wearing the insignia of the milicija or the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I don't know exactly what it said, whether it was the police of the Krajina or the police or milicija of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, something like that. But in any case, at that point I knew that that was not one of our soldiers but one of the soldiers from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe this uniform, the uniform of that soldier -- or actually, the police officer, not the soldier, according to what you say?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember. I remember very well the insignia because I thought that was one of our people, and then at the last moment when I saw what was written there, the Krajina milicija, I realised that I had to be careful how I spoke or how I addressed that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw that, what was your association when you saw that insignia on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Well, it didn't make me think of anything in particular. The person had this insignia on their sleeve, and to me that was an enemy soldier, somebody that I could not trust.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other police officers like that on that day or was that the only one that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I saw some other people in uniform, but I cannot tell you exactly what kind of insignia they had. There were different formations, so I don't know exactly which ones there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that this person could not have been a police officer of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina because the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was formed in 1992, would you accept my assertion?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I really don't know when the police force was formed, but that person did have a uniform with the insignia of the Krajina police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The state of the Serbian Republic of Krajina was formed in 1992. I was not talking about the police, but thank you. That is your comment. I have one more question relating to how you left the hospital. You said in your statement that you -- that there were four columns, a column for Zagreb, one for Novi Sad, one going to Belgrade, and a column of those people who wanted to stay in Vukovar. Is this correct about these four columns? And you stood in the column that was meant to go to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, it wasn't like that. There were no columns. We were just told to group, to make groups, of those who wanted to go to Zagreb, who wanted to stay in Vukovar, and a group of those what wanted to go to Serbia. I don't know if there was separate groups for those who wanted to go to Belgrade or Novi Sad. But in any case, there were groups for Zagreb, Serbia, and a group of those who wanted to stay in Vukovar, but there was no columns of any kind formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And my last question - I have to ask you this - was your husband of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: He never told me what he was, what his ethnicity was. We never talked about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we just proceed to the next cross-examination, there was a question by my learned friend where he indicated to the witness what the witness had said in the statement. It is at page 45, 11.41.07. And what is said, I think, from memory was that negotiations lasted from the 18th to the 20th of November. With the utmost respect, that is not what the -- certainly the English statement says, because the English statement said: "I heard that between the 18th and 20th of November that negotiations were still continuing." And there is, in my submission, a difference in relation to that. I don't know now if that is in relation to the B/C/S translation, but in the English translation that is certainly what I have. The second thing, again to assist my learned friend and I hope the Court, there was reference to a gentleman leaving at 2.00 p.m. In the English translation we have got 2.00 a.m. So again, I don't know if that assists all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, thank you for bringing that up at this point. Mr. Vasic, before we leave you, is there anything more you want to follow-up on either of those matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I would also like to thank my learned friend, but I think that I resolved the time-line issues with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it was night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the first issue raised, I simply asked the witness whether the negotiations were ongoing during this period of time. If my learned friend thinks that the use of continuous tense implies that it went on after the 20th, then I regret that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Polovina, good morning. My name is Mira Tapuskovic. I'm one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Miroslav Radic. I will try to speak slowly so that we ensure smooth interpretation and so that we can be sure that both my questions and your answers are accurately translated. I will also try not to repeat the questions put to you by Mr. Vasic; however, if there are such occasions when some questions are repeated, then that is due to my seeking clarification because I probably did not quite understand something from your previous answers. When you spoke earlier of your work at the radio station, at Vukovar Radio, which was later renamed Croatian Radio Vukovar, you mentioned Mirko Stankovic, the former editor-in-chief. Please tell me: Do you remember on what day his job was terminated?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what month it was when he was terminated?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to assist you and tell you it was in July of 1991, were you already employed then with the Croatian Radio Vukovar? You can't just nod.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, no, I was waiting for interpretation. I was employed in July. And as for the day of termination of Mirko Stankovic, I don't know. I never saw any official documents regarding that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you know that another person was appointed to his post as editor-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You even told us here the exact last name of that person.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was appointed by the new director, Mr. Serementa.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: The man's name is Zdravko Seremet. He was the new director of Croatian Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for mispronouncing the name; however, you and I understood each other. Would you please tell me now whether Mr. Seremet - I hope my pronunciation is right now - replaced Mr. Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Mr. Seremet was unable to replace Mirko Stankovic because Mirko Stankovic served as editor-in-chief. I think that was his post, whereas Zdravko Seremet was the radio's director.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Mr. Seremet submitted a disciplinary complaint against Mr. Stankovic, the former editor-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seremet - let me just try to refresh your memory - filed a disciplinary complaint to the disciplinary commission. There were a total of 15 of you working there when you started working full time, and some of you must have been members of this disciplinary commission. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: This is really the first time I hear of this. I really don't know what you're asking me. At the time, I did work at the radio station, but I have to correct you, it wasn't full time. However, I knew what was going on, but I cannot remember that there was any such disciplinary commission. I was certainly not a member of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We will not pursue this any longer since you, as you say, no nothing about these events. In the statement you gave to the investigators you said that immediately after the events in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, if I am not mistaken about the date, the HDZ took over control of the radio station. Can you please explain briefly to us what this means, that they took over control.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: That means, both physically and legally, from that time on the station was renamed into Croatian Radio Vukovar. I wasn't employed at the radio then. However, I heard from Sinisa Glavasevic and Branko, my husband, that the lock was changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your statement that between your two employments you spent a lot of time on the premises of Radio Vukovar and that you were quite familiar with what was going on in the entire area. Would you be able to tell us whether this pertains only to the city of Vukovar or to the entire Vukovar region, meaning Slavonija?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I would go to the premises of the radio station during the period of time when I wasn't employed then, because at the time I was dating my husband. The signal of Radio Vukovar was able to cover the territory of the municipality of Vukovar, and its programming concerned local issues, those of interest to the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm waiting for interpretation. Let me go back once again to Mr. Stankovic. He's a person who practically helped you get a job. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you said that he demonstrated some signs of Serb extremism. Today you said on page 4, line 6, that he was an editor with a pro-Serbian orientation and therefore there was no room for him at the radio station. Could you please tell us what this pro-Serbian programming orientation of his entailed.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Mirko Stankovic at the time was editor-in-chief, but nevertheless occasionally he would write a text either for the radio station or for the newspaper in Vukovar. These texts of his occasionally would send a message to the effect that Vukovar was a Serbian city and that the Serbian population was at risk. This is what indicated that his orientation was pro-Serbian. In addition to that, there were some 16.000 records at the radio station. Some of them were marked "airing prohibited." Those were the songs of Vice Vukov, Vera Svoboda, which means that those were the songs which were of Croatian content, something having to do with Croatia. When I asked about this, because I was shocked by this, I was told that this was a decision of Stankovic, decision not to air these songs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born in 1965?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who Vice Vukov was?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that he was convicted for his - let's put under quotation marks - his "nationalist outbursts." Do you remember that he was convicted for this?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Back then in 1971 or 1972, no, I didn't know that. Later on, when I was older, I learned about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the HDZ took over control and that all of a sudden the lock was changed. How did you learn that the lock had been changed? Who told you about this?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I think that I've already told you that Sinisa and Branko told me about this. Sinisa Glavasevic and Branko Polovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say why the lock had been changed and by whom?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: They didn't say the reason the lock was changed, but they mentioned people who were close to Tomislav Mercep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that people who were close to Tomislav Mercep also set the programming policy of the Croatian Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, if these people came and changed the lock?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. But that doesn't mean that they also set the programming policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you confirm that after the departure of Stankovic, Josip Esterajher became editor-in-chief? I hope I pronounced the name correctly.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: In the meantime, I remembered another man who spent a very brief amount of time there. I'm not quite sure, but I think his last name was Schlafhauser, and first name perhaps Kreso. I knew him very little, but I think that he spent a very short period of time serving as editor-in-chief between these two men. However, during the war, Josip Esterajher was editor-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you tell me does it seem strange to you that in a brief space of time, practically from the time you were re-employed at Croatian Radio Vukovar, four persons of Serb ethnicity holding prominent offices in town were replaced or fired?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know what persons you are talking about, and I also don't know whether they are of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When asked by my friend Vasic, you said you didn't know who the president of Vukovar municipality was. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I wasn't sure about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I tell you the name, Slavko Dokmanovic, would that sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also hear that on the 25th of July Franjo Tudjman disbanded the Municipal Assembly by a decree and also suspended Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Marin Vidic, Bili, replaced the director of the hospital, Rade Popovic, who was a Serb, on the 18th of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I know Marin Vidic, Bili, and the other one is a doctor, Rade Popovic, isn't he? I also heard of him. Now, as to whether he was replaced or not, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is important for us here is that he was the hospital director.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was the hospital director. I heard his name from other people. I know he was a doctor. I believe he was a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You as somebody employed at the radio station, somebody who is supposed to provide unbiased reports to the population in your area, did you know that a director of the large enterprise, Borovo, called Zdravko Egic, also a Serb, was also removed from office during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can have the usher's assistance now, please, to display a map. This is Exhibit 59, or proposed Exhibit 59. Your Honours, we shall have to take a break at some point. Do you think I should move on with my other questions now and leave the map for later, for after the break? Namely, I would like to ask the witness to mark the map and I would not wish to have to do that faster than necessary. So can I be allowed to change the original order of my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Certainly. Could I indicate that it's not a matter of finding the map, but the physical process of it being produced and able to be displayed, produced electronically, takes a great deal longer with a map than with a page of type face. But given the time, certainly move on to other questions and perhaps arrange with the court staff to have the map ready when we return after the break -- it is ready now, but I leave it to you entirely whether you want to deal with the map now. We would be breaking no later than quarter of an hour from now. If that isn't time enough to deal with the map, go on and deal with something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, Your Honour. I still remember your explanation about colour photographs requiring a little more time to be displayed on the screen, which is why I wanted to leave that for later. However, if we still have 15 minutes to go, I think that I can deal with the map or at least I'm sure that I will try to do my best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Polovina, do you have the map on your screen? You recognise it to be a map of Vukovar, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. All I can't see is the number that you referred to, 59.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's for internal use, so you needn't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please zoom in a little so that we may be better able to see the centre of Vukovar. A little more, please. More, more. Fine. That's excellent. Thank you very much. I want all the red dots to be displayed clearly on the screen so that the witness can see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Polovina, do you think you could give us a hand with this. I would like you to indicate certain buildings for us on the map or at least indicate their approximate location in Vukovar. The usher will help you with this.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I will tell you everything that I know. I must say, though, that I grew up in Borovo Naselje. I only came to Vukovar to live there in May 1991, and I'm not familiar with all the street names. I know some, but I can't say that I have a complete mastery of the town's layout and streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Polovina, you'll see it's actually much simpler than you'd expect. Can you please use the pointer to indicate for us on the map the location of what was first the main offices of Croatian Radio Vukovar and mark that as number 1. Approximately. I'm looking for an approximate location, not high precision. That's not what I'm expecting.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: The orange lines are the streets, I assume?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Those are the main roads in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: If this is the Vuka, then the workers' hall was here. And then about 300 metres further in this direction was our office. Here's a street that you turn into. You said to use number 1. Right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The Arabic numeral 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please blow that up a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now please indicate the direction of your studio.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: From this dot here in the direction of the Vuka, that's where the workers' hall was. Which number do you want me to use?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next Arabic numeral, 2. Put a number 2 there, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It was hereabouts, roughly speaking, the studio. I'm talking about the time when we were still able to transmit from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you for saying so on the transcript. Can you now put another dot marked with number 3 at the place or the area of Vukovar in which you lived after you had got married.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: That was a brief period, but -- is the water-tower somewhere on this map? Because if I know that I would find it much easier to find the exact location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't help you with this. You need to try and remember yourself.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I think it's hereabouts. Number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put a dot there, too, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please indicate what today you accurately called the headquarters of Vukovar's defence.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please put number 4 there.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It should be around here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next could you please use a dot and mark with number 5 the new shelter, the Vupik cellar that you were later to move to.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move that this map be admitted into evidence as our next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 127.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now please indicate -- or rather, we no longer need to indicate anything on the map, but can we please keep it on the screen for the time being. Now the map is gone. It's fine now. What I meant is -- well, regardless. Madam, we have now seen where your studio was and the shelter, too. Could you please tell us which route did you take to the hospital? You did tell us, after all, didn't you, that you would go very often from your radio office to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: When I say "we went to the hospital," I mean the Radio Vukovar team. I myself did not go as frequently as others, but I can still share that with you. The shelter you mentioned was the Vucedolska Kapljica shelter, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Number 5 is here, this is the main road, and the largest dot you can see in this area is the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you moved to the Vupik cellar; that was recorded today. You said you had decided to do that so as to be as near the hospital as possible. Why was that necessary for you to be as near the hospital as possible?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Funny, I don't remember saying that, about being near the hospital. We went to the municipal building to see Marin Vidic, Bili. That was perhaps one of the few cellars or the only shelter that was safe at the time in Vukovar, in as far as anything at all was safe in Vukovar at the time. But yes, we did wish to be as near the hospital as possible because that lessened the risk of us being killed. The shorter the route, the smaller the risk. One thing is to just run across a road and keep running for 300 or 400 metres. If you had to drive or walk for several kilometres, the chances of you surviving were very slim, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way from home to work, did you use any means of transport at all?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Which period are you referring to, because when the shelling was at its heaviest I wasn't staying at my house?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say "from home," then that must mean reference to the time while you were still there.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: For as long as I could, I either drove in a car or walked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go together with your husband or alone?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Sometimes we went together and sometimes I went on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the first severe shelling of town, the day which you defined as the beginning of fighting on the 25th of August -- or rather, since the first severe shelling, how was the distribution of food organised in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: From the 25th of August to sometime around the beginning of September, I was at the radio station and mostly we would cook our own food. No one brought us food. We organised everything ourselves because at this period every now and then you could still nip over and go to a shop to get some food. After that period -- after that period, it was very dangerous to walk around. It wasn't possible any longer, unless you had a death wish. It was very, very difficult. On some days there was nothing to eat. We had some old supplies, biscuits, canned food, pate. It was extremely difficult. But people who organised food distribution in Vukovar had not yet gotten into their stride, as it were. But this began to work much better after a while, and we heard that food distribution was organised in some of the shelters. You knew exactly who was doing the cooking and who was bringing in the food supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Food was being prepared at Borovo Komerc?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Some, yes. I did hear that, that was one of the places. Borovo Komerc did not organise food for the entire town, but yes, people were cooking food there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This food was then distributed to certain areas in Vukovar, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was on a daily basis that food from Borovo Komerc was being delivered to other parts of Vukovar, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know about other parts of Vukovar, but while we were at Vucedolska Kapljica, for a while we were receiving food from Borovo Komerc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My conclusion, Madam, would be that it was not that dangerous, after all, to move around if you were able to organise food distribution all over Vukovar on a daily basis. Would that not seem to be a fair conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I myself don't need to have any conclusions at all because I know the facts. I don't know their numbers, but people were getting killed on a daily basis in the process. One day there would be someone who got killed. The next day it was someone else, and then two or five people were killed in the possess as they were delivering food across Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know whether these people were killed by shells or also mines?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know about the various ways in which these people were killed. Shells certainly killed some of them. I could also assume that maybe some of the roads were booby-trapped and that there were mines, unexploded mines, along those roads that killed some of the drivers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is a good time to have a break, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Polovina, I would like to put one more question to you at the point where we stopped before the break regarding the functioning of the town, in that period, as you say of the siege. My colleague Vasic reminded you of your interview to Slobodna Dalmacija on the occasion of the 10th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us here that already in September 1991 all the food reserves in the Nama department store were removed, placed under control, for the purpose of distribution in the shelters?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I cannot be 100 per cent certain whether this was in September, but I think that it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether movement was restricted in town in the morning and in the evening.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: In which period?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the September and October period, the ninth and the tenth month.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It was restricted because of the shelling. So I don't understand. When you say the evening hours or daytime, I think it's the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking whether perhaps movement was restricted or not allowed after nightfall, after 10.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution you said that until the 15th of September, is that correct, the ninth month?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was still possible to move around town, although movement was restricted. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So movement was restricted, as far as you're concerned, because of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You confirmed that you knew Marin Vidic, Bili, and that you kept in touch with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Marin and he did work as a liaison -- oh, and the radio station was in contact with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you confirm that the Main Staff adopted any kind of decision relating to restriction of movement?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember. The only thing I do remember is that I had absolutely no desire to go out because there was shooting. I think that I could have done that at any point, though, but I would have risked my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that it was obvious from my question that I was referring to a formal restriction of movement. Do you know if there was any kind of formal imposition on restricting movement past?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the usher to call up document number 0D04-0001. That's the number of the B/C/S version. Could that be please placed on the ELMO and the screen in front of the witness. The English version has the number 0D04-0003. Could the witness be shown the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be possible to zoom in on the document and could we look at the first -- the top half of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the date from the top left corner of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I -- from what I can see, it says 8th of September, 1991. I don't know if there are any other numbers in front of the 8th, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please read to us the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, shouldn't the witness be asked if this is a document that she knows and has personal knowledge of? If she does not have personal knowledge of the document, how can she give any useful evidence in relation to its content?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much. I agree with my learned friend's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Polovina, did you have the opportunity to familiarise yourself with this document?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No. I've never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show us page 2 of the document. Could the witness please tell us whether she can read who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see anyone's signature, but I can see the name "Marin Vidic, Bili" in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There is no signature on the decision, but there is a stamp. Can you read just one line. It's the last-but-one line on the second page of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I repeat my objection. If the witness doesn't know the document, has not seen the document, what is the relevance pursuant to the question, and how can this witness then give any useful evidence in relation to it? It's not her document, she doesn't know the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my previous question to the witness had to do with the restriction of movement within the town. The witness said that she didn't know about that, but she confirmed that Radio Vukovar or that they had land-line with Marin Vidic, Bili; they were in contact with him. This is a decision that relates to the whole of Vukovar and also would include the conduct and the work of the radio station. I believe that if the witness were to see the document, perhaps she would remember -- if not having seen this document, then perhaps having commented on the document perhaps with her colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore, the document, I believe, can be properly put to the witness to see whether it prompts her recollection of the situation at the time. If it doesn't, it can't be taken beyond that. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that you've now read the document. Do you maybe remember commenting the decision to restrict movement in Vukovar with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember this document, and I don't remember commenting with my colleagues about what is written in the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps comment with your colleagues about some changes in broadcasting policy in conditions of war?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Did you perhaps comment with your colleagues any kind of need to change the broadcasting of news programmes in conditions of war?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the witness has said that she is not familiar with this document, I'm not going to seek to admit the document at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your first shelter which was under the staircase in the studio radio -- studio building, that you left that shelter on the 15th of September. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No. Firstly, it wasn't a shelter. It was just a basement. And it was the newsroom building, not the studio building, and we didn't leave it on the 15th of September but it was on the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you went to a new shelter, to the basement of the Vupik enterprise. Can you please tell us what the Vupik company was, what was their business?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Vupik had several departments, farming, wine growing, crop growing. Probably had its own shops. I don't know really that much about this company, but these are the things that I know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you entered the Vupik warehouse, what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: It was a warehouse that we used as a shelter. It was a large, empty space. I remember that there was wine there. That's all I remember. Wine, water, some kind of mineral water, Donat mineral water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Donat is a brand of mineral water?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who told you and who permitted you to move to the Vupik warehouse and to use it as a shelter as well as a place of work.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: After the withdrawal on the 15th of October, first of all we came to the municipal building where Marin Vidic, Bili, was. And my editors, having agreed on that with him first, decided that the most appropriate shelter for us would be this Vucedolska Kapljica, this space owned by Vupik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the defence staff of Vukovar directly admitted you to this area?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No. Marin Vidic, Bili, at the time was the commissioner for the municipality of Vukovar. So it was a kind of mayor's post; he was not a military person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain why you said "a military person."

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Because you said. I'm sorry, I'm speeding up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that a military person admitted you to Vupik's cellar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No. You suggested an answer like that to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not mention any word that could associate with any kind of military person or unit. Could you please tell me who from the municipality, somebody charged by the commissioner, Marin Vidic, or somebody from the Vukovar defence staff that admitted you to the Vupik cellar. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember who it was. I don't know if anybody was there in that capacity at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, somebody had to give you the key.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: The cellar didn't have a key. You took some steps from the yard down into the cellar. It was an open area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that until the 15th of October, nobody of the citizens from Vukovar actually was using that large cellar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know whether anybody used the basement until the 15th of October, because I had never been to that basement prior to that. When we arrived on the 15th of October, it was empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now sum up what you told us twice today. Following your entry into the Vupik basement on the 15th of October, who else came to that basement and when to share that space with you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Several days after we entered the basement some people came who, until that time, had been in a shelter in Sajmiste. When Sajmiste fell, people started withdrawing into the centre of town, and thus arrived in our basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Perhaps 80 to 100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So together with you from Croatian Radio Vukovar, how many people were there all together, using that basement?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: As I've told you there were 80 to 100 of them, whereas there were - just a minute - six people working at the radio. That means that it was between 86 and 106 people. Sinisa, Branko, Alenka, myself, and so on. There were six or seven of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you said that soldiers also came to you. Can you tell us who were these soldiers who came to visit you.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember all of the names. There were some soldiers. I remember some of them who had come to Vukovar from various parts of Croatia to defend the town. I remember one young man who was from the vicinity of Sinj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Members of the 204th Vukovar Battalion also came. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: At the time I'm not sure that that unit was in existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In October?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they come from Vinkovci and Osijek?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Nobody came in October. But now that we're discussing the soldiers who occasionally came to the basement, then I'm referring to the young men who would come to Vukovar back in August or September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since your task was to provide information to the residents, you told us yourself that you acquired information in various ways, by going out to various places.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that was still not too dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you acquired information via telephone?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you must have had information of -- about all of the people who came from various places to assist in the defence of Vukovar. What units were there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I really don't know what units came to assist in the defence of Vukovar. But I know that they were from various parts of Croatia. I remember that there were people from Dalmacia, from Zagorije, from Dubrovnik. One could tell that based on their pronunciation. However, I don't know their names or the units they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned Sinj. How far is Sinj from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: As the crow flies or using highways?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nobody could have flown to Vukovar at that time, so let's say travelling on highways. What was the distance?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I think that Vukovar-Zagreb is 275 kilometres, and then Zagreb-Sien, perhaps 300. I'm not sure. But around -- more than 500 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So practically people had come from all over Croatia to join the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. There were people there from various parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You must have had information on the approximate number of such people.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I did not have such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you told the investigators about Croatian Radio Vukovar and the relations with the staff, you said that you did not have the best of rapport with them. Can you please tell us what were the differences in opinion between you and the defence staff.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We had very good relations with the commander, Dedakovic, and Branko Borkovic. Initially when the defence was being organised after the events in Borovo Selo, the person in charge was Tomislav Mercep then. And in that initial stage of war, if I can call it that, it took us some time to get accustomed to the situation because none of us from the radio had experienced war and neither did any of these defenders. Perhaps some of the older people had some war experience, but nobody else. So we didn't know how to operate under the circumstances. The war began and we couldn't really find our footing right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you didn't tell me what was exactly the difference in the position, that of your radio station and the defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I could give the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need the statement. There was no difference of opinion or position. Simply put, we wanted to acquire information on how the defence was being organised. Naturally the commander refused to give us that information for security of the people in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you went to get your information in the staff and also at the hospital. Would you please tell me, Mrs. Polovina -- when I say "you," I don't necessarily mean you yourself but employees of Radio Vukovar. Would you please tell me what type of information you received at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: The number of the wounded, dead, lack of medication, blood supplies, there were also times when the hospital had been shelled. So that type of information we acquired at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you transmitted this information daily to Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you send it to? To the medical staff? Ministry -- Ministry of Health?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No. We had contacts with -- or rather, we sent our reports solely to the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your reports -- then somebody in Zagreb refused to publicly publish or announce your reports. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Some of the reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned the arrival of Vesna Bosanac and Bili to the Vupik basement, you also said that several employees of the post office brought in some equipment. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was an amplifier there or some other type of equipment, a loud-speaker or an amplifier. That's what you said. That's what's recorded in the transcript. Would you please tell us with greater degree of accuracy what equipment was brought in from the post office.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember, and I'm not really very knowledgeable when it comes to equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of your testimony that you would frequently come to Croatian Radio Vukovar to help your husband, who was a technician.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. You mean while I wasn't employed there? Yes, I used to come then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So after being a journalist and a reporter for so many years, you still don't know what an amplifier or a loud-speaker is?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I know what those things are, but I don't know whether lads from the post office had that type of equipment. All I know is they got the telephone connection up and running. I don't know how they did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you tell us why was the link with Zagreb established from the Vupik basement and not from the building of the post office? Was it because the defence staff had been relocated to the Vupik basement?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: At that time there was nobody from the defence staff there. They had left the city. Our basement, the Vupik basement, was very near the staff premises. And I think that this was the closest spot or the most logical location for establishing the telephone connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that the entire staff had left the city, attempting to break through?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "the entire staff." The people who were there in that location, commander and people around him. They were the people who had left the premises of the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you know for a fact that it was impossible to establish telephone link with Zagreb from the post office building?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that there was just one telephone in Vukovar during the last days or the the last two weeks before the fall of town?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the information I had at the time, yes. I was told that there was just one telephone in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Marin Vidic, Bili, stated that pursuant to his order on the 1st of November, all telephone lines in Vukovar were disconnected, leaving just one telephone operational?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us then: Where was this single telephone located in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: At that moment, while we were in the basement when the young men from the post office came, that was the telephone that was operational.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please describe to us the dimensions of the Vupik basement. How big were the barrels?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't remember there being any barrels. I remember wine bottles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you define in any way the space of that basement?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I think it was a bit smaller than this room, if we're talking about square metres; however, it wasn't the same shape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are now referring to this courtroom, Courtroom III?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know how many times you or any of your colleagues met with Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I met her very rarely. I seldom went to the hospital or, for that matter, left the basement to go anywhere, whereas my colleagues were in contact with her more frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your colleague Vesna Vukovic among them?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know on what occasion or for what reasons she met Vesna Bosanac? Did she tell you what she had talked about with her?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: She went there as a journalist to acquire information about the situation at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Sajmiste at one point in time during the siege fell?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say how many residents lived in that part of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No, I can't. Maybe I could tell you what my assessment is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you say about 2.000 residents under siege? If you know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: That sounds reasonable. It certainly wasn't 100.000. It could have been 2.000, easily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who reached the Vupik shelter from Sajmiste, did those people tell you why they were now moving to your shelter?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. They said that the defence lines at Sajmiste had been pierced, that the Serbs were entering houses and people just fled back towards the centre where they felt they might be safer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your job was to keep the citizens informed, wasn't it? You knew at any point in time who controlled which area of Vukovar, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: This was by no means always the case. Sometimes we ourselves didn't have the right information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the MUP and ZNG forces in Vukovar, did they control the area known as Petrova Gora also?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have two or three questions left before I close and complete my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you know about the daily paper, Glas Slavonije?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the owner is of that particular publication?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two or three days before your testimony, I surfed their web site. On the 26th of November on their web site, they published a list of all hospital employees during the siege, including all the help workers, including the people who helped with the logistics. When it comes to liaison and coordination, the names given are you, your husband, the late Sinisa Glavasevic, and Vesna Vukovic. Vesna Bosanac expresses her gratitude to you all for the assistance that you extended. Would I be wrong in concluding that both you and your Croatian Radio Vukovar [as interpreted] were placed directly at the disposal of the hospital in order to disguise the presence of ZNG members and all the paramilitaries who were there in the hospital in Vukovar just before the fall?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: I find your sentence a trifle too lengthy, perhaps. If you could please repeat your question. You said: Would I be wrong -- well, you are suggesting that my colleagues and myself from Radio Vukovar were placed at the disposal of the -- the sentence was a bit long, but if I can sum it up. Yes, you are wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your -- the work and services in terms of providing information. Did you offer your services to the hospital, which on the eve of Vukovar's fall had been hiding ZNG members and paramilitaries, soldiers, such as members of the 2004th [as interpreted] Vukovar Battalion and ZNG units?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We did enjoy the hospital's support ourselves. Likewise, we returned this support to the hospital by sending messages out to Zagreb and to the world at large about everything that was going on in the Vukovar Hospital. As for the latter part of your sentence, well, I wouldn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Zagreb refused to receive your information.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: That was indeed the case at one point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question is in relation to the moment at which you were leaving the shelter. There was still lots of civilians remaining in Vukovar, weren't there, on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why then did the entire Radio Vukovar team decided to try to escape? Was there a reason for you to attempt to escape?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: We knew that the town had fallen on the 18th of November. We were scared of what might befall us. There weren't too many options open to us, but one of them was to try and escape. So this was an option that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So much like the staff members several days before, the entire team of Radio Vukovar decided to break through the siege and escape Vukovar. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA
utterances.text: Those from the staff had gone on before us, the day before, and we decided to give it a thought, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Obviously that now is the time when we need to adjourn for the day. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. Your Honour, there is an important administrative matter that we have to deal with tomorrow morning. We have not made any application before for a delay in the trial. I wonder if it would be possible if we could start or commence tomorrow morning at 10.00, as opposed to 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It happens, Mr. Moore, that that would also suit the convenience of the Chamber. So you needn't argue too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In fact, it would be even more convenient at 10.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you've relieved me of a problem about tomorrow morning as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of that, we will resume tomorrow morning at 10.15 rather than 9.00. Thank you. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
